Name: Goal and win condition
OneLine: The state that ends the game and says who won.
TryIt: Play tic-tac-toe, then change the goal: whoever makes three in a row loses.
BuildIt: A `/stage` page that watches one number and fires an end cue when it is reached.
AiAngle: Who sets the AI's goal, and can anyone change it? A fixed, trivial goal is the paperclip maximizer; a goal the players must name is alignment.
InOurGame: yes: every version (Data Center ends on the AI's share of the map or the last round; The Committee and Normal Technology the same way)
Source: GM card 1 (tdm155ai-week-11, Nov 13); TDM 98 small-rooms mechanics (Nov 5)
Definition: The condition, set before play starts, that ends the game and says who has won, lost or drawn. Because it names what players are after, it decides which moves count as good ones.
Description:
In games:

- **[Chess](../games/chess.md)**: Checkmate ends the game at once, whatever material either side still has, so a player can be far ahead and still lose. [2]
- **[Monopoly](../games/monopoly.md)**: The last player who is not bankrupt wins, so the game is won by ruining the others rather than by getting rich. [3]
- **[Pandemic](../games/pandemic.md)**: The players win together by curing all four diseases, and lose together in any of three ways (too many outbreaks, too few disease cubes, too few player cards left to draw). [4]
- **[Data Center](../games/data-center.md)**: The AI wins when it holds half the region's nodes; the humans survive if the ten rounds run out first, and then check each faction's private goal. [5]

**Shows it** (GM's card): Chess (checkmate) [1]

**With AI** (HI): Who sets the AI's goal, and can anyone change it? A fixed, trivial goal is the paperclip maximizer; a goal the players must name is alignment. [1]

**In our game** (Nov 14 rulesets): yes: every version (Data Center ends on the AI's share of the map or the last round; The Committee and Normal Technology the same way) [1]
HowTo:
**Try it in two minutes** (GM's card): Play tic-tac-toe, then change the goal: whoever makes three in a row loses. [1]

**Build it** (GM's card): A `/stage` page that watches one number and fires an end cue when it is reached. [1]
WhyTo:
**Proposed, for Marlon to choose:**

1. Rewrite a familiar game's goal (tic-tac-toe where three in a row loses, as GM's card has it) to show students that the goal, not the pieces, sets what the game is about.
2. In a game about AI, ask who wrote the AI's goal and who can change it; the win condition is where the alignment question becomes a rule.
3. Use it as the first question of a close reading: what does this game count as winning, and what does that leave out?
HomeGameClassroom:
**Proposed, for Marlon to choose:**

1. Play any short game twice, once with its goal and once with an inverted goal, and compare how people played.
2. Groups write a win condition on an index card for a shared board; the class plays whichever card is drawn.
HomeGameDigital:
**Proposed, for Marlon to choose:**

1. A one-number web page (a shared counter) with an end condition the class sets before play.
2. Ask Claude to change only the win condition of a small browser game and play the two versions side by side.

Definition: The short cycle of actions a player repeats throughout a game, around which the rest of the game is built. Each pass through the loop changes the state a little and sets up the next pass.
Description:
In games:

- **[Universal Paperclips](../games/universal-paperclips.md)**: Make clips, sell them, buy wire and clip-making machines with the money, make more clips; later stages keep the loop and change what it is made of. [2]
- **[Tetris](../games/tetris.md)**: A piece falls, the player turns and places it, full lines clear, and the next piece falls. [3]
- **[League of Legends](../games/league-of-legends.md)**: Kill minions for gold, go back to base to buy items, return to fight stronger; the ENGL 189VG brainstorm names it as an example of a loop. [4]
- **[Data Center](../games/data-center.md)**: Each round the AI draws a card, upkeep runs, then each faction acts; ten rounds of the same cycle. [5][6]

**Shows it** (GM's card): *Universal Paperclips* (make, sell, invest) [1]

**With AI** (HI): The AI's loop runs on its own beside the players' loop; the drama is where the two meet. [1]

Name: Combat
OneLine: A contest between characters or units, resolved by skill, numbers or dice.
ShowsIt: League of Legends; God of War; Risk's dice battles
TryIt: Two players, two numbers each (strength, health); take turns rolling a die and subtracting.
BuildIt: Health and damage as numbers on each unit, a resolve function, and feedback when a hit lands.
AiAngle: The default loop of video games; what would a game about AI look like without it?
Definition: A contest between characters or units in which each tries to damage or defeat the other, resolved by the player's skill, by numbers, or by dice.
Description:
In games:

- **[League of Legends](../games/league-of-legends.md)**: Champions fight minions, towers and each other, and gold from kills buys the items that make the next fight easier. [2]
- **[God of War (2018)](../games/god-of-war-2018.md)**: Kratos fights at close range with the axe and his fists, and at a distance by throwing the axe. [3]
- **[Risk](../games/risk.md)**: Battles are dice rolls: the attacker rolls up to three dice and the defender up to two, ties going to the defender. [4]

**Shows it** (EG's row): League of Legends; God of War; Risk's dice battles [1]

**With AI** (EG's row): The default loop of video games; what would a game about AI look like without it? [1]

**In our game** (Nov 14 rulesets): no [1]
HowTo:
**Try it in two minutes** (EG's row): Two players, two numbers each (strength, health); take turns rolling a die and subtracting. [1]

**Build it** (EG's row): Health and damage as numbers on each unit, a resolve function, and feedback when a hit lands. [1]
WhyTo: The ENGL 189VG brainstorm treats combat as the default loop of video games and asks "what would be a loop that's not combat?" [5]
Author: EG (Claude Code 10549f6d-2ac5-41cc-9ae5-5682cc105485, started in ll-week-11 on FAS-DDW32PXW5L), Nov 17

Name: The map tells the story
OneLine: Where things are, and the route through them, carry the story; the map can also record what happened.
ShowsIt: The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild; Dark Souls; Risk boards after a game
TryIt: Draw a map of five places on 11x17 paper; each place reveals one line of a story when visited.
BuildIt: Places as nodes with text; visiting a node logs it, and the log is the story.
AiAngle: An AI's spread across a map is a story told by where it is.
InOurGame: partly: the region map shows where the AI has spread
Source: ENGL 189VG brainstorm and planning (HackMD, english-189vg-initial-brainstorming, lines 23–27; eng 189vg planning, lines 20–22); Jenkins, 'Game Design as Narrative Architecture'
Definition: The places in a game, and the routes through them, tell its story: the player learns what happened by where things are and what they find there. The map can also become a record of what the player did.
Description:
Henry Jenkins calls this 'narrative architecture', with game designers as builders of story spaces. [4]

In games:

- **[The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild](../games/zelda-breath-of-the-wild.md)**: Link wakes a century after Ganon turned the Guardians against Hyrule, and regains his memories by returning to places from his past. [2]
- **[Dark Souls](../games/dark-souls.md)**: Item descriptions and the look of the world tell the history of Lordran, a decaying kingdom, without pulling the player out of the game for story. [3]

**Shows it** (EG's row): The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild; Dark Souls; Risk boards after a game [1]

**With AI** (EG's row): An AI's spread across a map is a story told by where it is. [1]

**In our game** (Nov 14 rulesets): partly: the region map shows where the AI has spread [1]
HowTo:
**Try it in two minutes** (EG's row): Draw a map of five places on 11x17 paper; each place reveals one line of a story when visited. [1]

**Build it** (EG's row): Places as nodes with text; visiting a node logs it, and the log is the story. [1]
WhyTo: The ENGL 189VG planning: "maps spatialize development of plot", and can be "a record of the story (this character did this, then that, then that)". [5]
Author: EG (Claude Code 10549f6d-2ac5-41cc-9ae5-5682cc105485, started in ll-week-11 on FAS-DDW32PXW5L), Nov 17

ShowsIt: Super Mario Bros.' jump; any Unity scene with a gravity setting
TryIt: Toss a ball, then a balloon, then a paper airplane: same throw, different physics.
BuildIt: Open a Unity scene, change jump velocity or gravity in the Inspector, and play it again.

Description:
In games:

- **[Super Mario Bros.](../games/super-mario-bros.md)**: How high Mario jumps depends on how long the jump button is held, and he speeds up smoothly from a walk to a run. [2]
- **[Portal](../games/portal.md)**: Momentum carries through a portal, so the player gains speed by falling into one portal and flies out of the other. [3]

Name: Mechanics tell the story
OneLine: What the player can do (the verbs) carries the game's meaning and plot, apart from its text.
ShowsIt: Papers, Please; Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons; The Legend of Zelda (the sword as the first gift)
TryIt: Take a story everyone knows and give it one verb; play it, then change the verb.
BuildIt: Change what the player can do at a turning point in the story, not what the screen says.
AiAngle: What does a game about AI let the humans do? The verbs are its argument.

Source: ENGL 189VG planning (HackMD, eng 189vg planning, lines 17–18: 'rules as narrative structure', 'using mechanics to develop/uncover plot')

Description:
In games:

- **[Papers, Please](../games/papers-please.md)**: The player is a border inspector checking documents against a growing list of rules, and stamping papers brings constant moral choices that make it hard to be good. [3]
- **[Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons](../games/brothers-a-tale-of-two-sons.md)**: Each brother is steered with one side of the controller, and late in the game that division of the controls becomes part of the story's ending. [4]
- **[Animal Crossing](../games/animal-crossing.md)**: Paying off the house loan earns a bigger house and a bigger loan, so the game argues about debt without saying a word (Bogost, as quoted in the glossary). [2]

**Shows it** (EG's row): Papers, Please; Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons; The Legend of Zelda (the sword as the first gift) [1]

**With AI** (EG's row): What does a game about AI let the humans do? The verbs are its argument. [1]

**In our game** (Nov 14 rulesets): yes: the factions' actions (harden, protest, sell) are the game's claims [1]
HowTo:
**Try it in two minutes** (EG's row): Take a story everyone knows and give it one verb; play it, then change the verb. [1]

**Build it** (EG's row): Change what the player can do at a turning point in the story, not what the screen says. [1]
WhyTo: The ENGL 189VG planning: "rules as narrative structure", "using mechanics to develop/uncover plot". [5]

Name: The move updates state
OneLine: A move is a small record of what a player did; the game state is every move so far applied, in order, to the start.
ShowsIt: Chess notation (a game is its list of moves); ES's study 01; the LL's NFC taps
TryIt: Play tic-tac-toe while one person writes each move on a card; then rebuild the board from the cards alone.
BuildIt: Store moves as rows in a log and compute the board from them; replaying part of the log shows the board at any earlier moment.
AiAngle: An AI player's move is one more row; reading the log is how a model catches up on a game.
InOurGame: yes: the play page logs each phase and action, and the state follows from them
Source: ES's study 01 (_content/mechanics/studies/01-the-move-updates-state/); Marlon's 07:42 concept inventory, items 13 and 17
Definition: A move is a small record of what one player did at one moment, and the game state is what you get by applying every move so far, in order, to the starting position. Sicart's definition of mechanics as methods that act on the game state is the reading behind it.
Description:
ES's study 01 illustrates it with tic-tac-toe in which every click is a row and a slider unbuilds the board. [7]

In games:

- **[Chess](../games/chess.md)**: A game can be written down as its list of moves in notation, which lets a reader play through the game again. [4]
- **[Every tap is a row (prototype)](../games/proto-every-tap-is-a-row.md)**: Every tap writes a row, and the board is only those rows replayed. [5]
- **[Data Center](../games/data-center.md)**: Each AI card, vote and faction action changes the saved state, which the play page keeps in the browser. [6]

**Shows it** (EG's row): Chess notation (a game is its list of moves); ES's study 01; the LL's NFC taps [1]

**With AI** (EG's row): An AI player's move is one more row; reading the log is how a model catches up on a game. [1]

**In our game** (Nov 14 rulesets): yes: the play page logs each phase and action, and the state follows from them [1]
HowTo:
**Try it in two minutes** (EG's row): Play tic-tac-toe while one person writes each move on a card; then rebuild the board from the cards alone. [1]

**Build it** (EG's row): Store moves as rows in a log and compute the board from them; replaying part of the log shows the board at any earlier moment. [1]
WhyTo:
